title: Why Accessibility Matters
summary: Accessibility serves a far larger and more varied group of people than "screen reader users," and the business case for investing in it is concrete, not charitable. Learn who it serves and why the case holds up under scrutiny.

slides.markdown:
A common misconception walks in the door before this topic even starts: that accessibility means "support for screen readers," a narrow feature for a small, separate group of users. That framing undercounts who's actually affected and overstates how separate the work is from building a good product at all.

Accessibility is about making sure a product's functionality doesn't depend on having full vision, full hearing, fine motor control, or complete attention available at the moment someone is using it — conditions that are far more common, and far more situational, than the stereotype suggests.

This topic sets up the rest of the group: who accessibility actually serves, the assistive technology landscape beyond screen readers, and the concrete business and legal reasons it isn't optional in a serious engineering org.

slides.subTitle: Permanent, temporary, and situational
slides.markdown:
Disability isn't one fixed category — a useful model splits it into three durations, and most people experience all three at different points:

- **Permanent** — someone who is blind, deaf, or has a motor impairment that doesn't change. This is the group most people picture first, and it's the smallest of the three.
- **Temporary** — a broken arm in a cast, an ear infection, eye surgery recovery. The impairment is real and the same accommodations help, but it resolves over weeks or months.
- **Situational** — a parent holding a baby in one arm, someone in bright sunlight unable to read low-contrast text, a user in a loud room who can't play audio, someone on a spotty connection where images fail to load and alt text is the only content that arrives.

The same fix — captions, sufficient contrast, keyboard operability, meaningful alt text — serves all three groups simultaneously. A permanently deaf user and someone on a train without headphones both need captions; building for one covers the other for free.

slides.subTitle: Beyond screen readers
slides.markdown:
Screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, TalkBack) are the assistive technology most engineers have heard of, but the landscape is much wider, and each tool depends on different things from your code:

- **Screen readers** — read the page aloud using the accessibility tree; depend on semantic HTML and correct ARIA.
- **Switch devices** — a single button (or a few) that a user with limited mobility presses to step through focusable elements sequentially; depend entirely on a correct, logical tab order and every interactive element actually being reachable by keyboard.
- **Screen magnifiers** (ZoomText and OS-level zoom) — used by low-vision users who don't need a screen reader at all; depend on layouts that reflow sanely at high zoom instead of clipping or requiring horizontal scroll in both directions.
- **Voice control** (Dragon, Voice Control) — lets users say "click submit" to activate a button by its visible label; depends on the visible label and the accessible name actually matching, since the software matches spoken text against the accessible name.

Each of these fails differently if you get the underlying markup wrong — which is why "screen reader support" alone is an incomplete accessibility bar.

slides.sectionTitle: The spectrum of disability and assistive tech
slides.markdown:
Mapping disability types against the assistive tech that helps makes the breadth concrete in one view: visual impairments range from full blindness (screen readers) through low vision (magnifiers, high contrast) to color blindness (never relying on color alone to convey meaning). Motor impairments range from no fine motor control (switch devices, voice control) to temporary limits like a broken arm (keyboard-only navigation, larger touch targets). Auditory impairments span full deafness (captions, transcripts) to situational noise (same fix). Cognitive and attention differences benefit from consistent navigation patterns, plain language, and generous time limits (or none at all) on interactions.

The throughline across every branch: none of these technologies are exotic add-ons layered onto a website after the fact — they consume the same DOM structure, the same semantic HTML, and the same ARIA that a well-built page already needs for other reasons.

slides.subTitle: Market reach, SEO overlap, retention
slides.markdown:
The business case doesn't need to lean on goodwill — it holds up on numbers alone. The WHO estimates roughly 1 in 6 people globally live with a significant disability; that's a meaningful fraction of any product's addressable market being actively excluded by inaccessible design, not a rounding error.

There's real overlap with SEO too, not a coincidence: search engine crawlers and screen readers both depend on the same underlying signals — meaningful heading structure, descriptive link text, alt text on images, semantic landmarks. A page built to be accessible is, almost as a side effect, built to be well-understood by a crawler, and vice versa; "click here" links and image-only content with no alt text hurt both a screen reader user and a search ranking simultaneously.

There's also a retention angle rarely discussed explicitly: a user who hits an inaccessible barrier once — can't complete checkout with a screen reader, can't tab through a broken modal — usually doesn't file a bug report, they just leave and don't come back, which never shows up as a support ticket but shows up in the numbers eventually as unexplained churn.

Accessibility litigation is not a theoretical risk — it's an active, well-established category, with the US alone seeing thousands of ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) web-accessibility lawsuits filed per year, and similar legal frameworks in place across the EU (the European Accessibility Act), the UK, Canada, and elsewhere.

Courts in the US have repeatedly held that the ADA's public-accommodation requirements extend to websites and apps, not just physical spaces — a ruling that surprises engineers who assume "the ADA is about wheelchair ramps" and don't realize it reaches their product. WCAG (covered in depth later in this group) is the technical standard most of these legal frameworks point to as the practical bar for compliance, which is part of why WCAG conformance shows up in vendor security/compliance questionnaires and enterprise procurement contracts even for companies with no direct legal exposure yet.

The pragmatic framing for an engineering team: legal risk is a real, board-level reason accessibility gets funded, even on top of the product and ethical reasons — and it's usually cheaper to build features accessibly from the start than to retrofit and settle a claim later.

slides.subTitle: Accessible design helping everyone
slides.markdown:
The term comes from a literal example: curb cuts (the small ramps at sidewalk corners) were built for wheelchair users, but end up used constantly by parents with strollers, delivery workers with hand trucks, travelers with rolling luggage, and cyclists — the accommodation for one group turned out to help nearly everyone.

The same pattern shows up constantly in software: captions, built for deaf users, get used by anyone watching a video in a quiet office or a loud commute without headphones. Keyboard shortcuts, built for users who can't use a mouse precisely, get adopted by power users because they're faster than clicking. High-contrast text, needed by low-vision users, is also just easier to read for everyone in bright sunlight on a phone screen. Clear, simple language, needed by users with cognitive disabilities or reading in a non-native language, is also just better writing for everyone.

The curb-cut effect is a genuinely useful argument in a prioritization conversation — accessibility work rarely benefits only the group it was designed for, which changes the ROI calculation most teams implicitly (and wrongly) assume.

slides.sectionTitle: The myth that it's only about screen readers
slides.markdown:
Teams that treat accessibility as "add ARIA labels and test with VoiceOver" reliably ship products that still fail for large groups of disabled users, because the fix set for a screen reader user and the fix set for, say, a keyboard-only user or a low-vision user are only partially overlapping.

A concrete failure this produces: a component gets `aria-label`s added everywhere (satisfying a screen-reader-only mental model) while its custom dropdown still can't be operated with the Tab/arrow/Escape keys at all — perfectly announced by a screen reader, completely unusable by a switch-device user or anyone who simply can't use a mouse. Screen-reader-only thinking also misses color-contrast failures entirely (screen readers don't care about contrast), and misses time-limit issues entirely (a session timeout that's fine for a screen reader user can be a hard barrier for someone with a cognitive disability who needs longer to complete a form).

The corrective framing: accessibility work should be scoped against the actual range of disabilities and assistive tech from earlier in this topic, not collapsed down to whichever single tool (usually a screen reader) happens to be the one most engineers have heard of or tried once.

A common, understandable misconception is that accessibility is a separate audit phase — something a specialist or a tool checks near the end of a project, layered on top of otherwise-finished work. In practice the cheapest and most durable accessibility comes from decisions made at build time: choosing `<button>` over `<div onclick>`, writing meaningful alt text as an image is added rather than backfilling it later, picking a color palette that clears contrast requirements from the design stage rather than patching individual components after a failed audit.

Retrofitting accessibility into a shipped product is measurably more expensive than building it in from the start, for the same reason retrofitting any cross-cutting concern is expensive — every component built without it needs individual review and rework, versus every new component simply inheriting the right defaults from a design system and a set of team habits.

The rest of this group covers exactly those build-time habits: semantic HTML, correct ARIA usage, keyboard and focus management, accessible forms, and the testing practices that catch what habits alone miss.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering "why should we invest in this"
slides.markdown:
A strong answer to this question in an interview or a real prioritization meeting layers the case rather than leaning on just one argument, because different stakeholders respond to different parts of it:

1. **Scale** — roughly 1 in 6 people globally have a significant disability, and permanent, temporary, and situational impairments together touch nearly everyone at some point.
2. **Legal exposure** — ADA and equivalent web-accessibility litigation is active and well-established, not hypothetical.
3. **The curb-cut effect** — most accessibility work improves the product for users who aren't disabled at all, which changes the ROI math.
4. **Cost asymmetry** — building it in from the start is reliably cheaper than retrofitting after an audit or a complaint surfaces the gap.

Leading with only the compliance/legal angle tends to read as covering yourself rather than building a better product; leading with only the ethical angle can get dismissed as not tied to business outcomes. Naming all four together is what actually moves a prioritization conversation.
